title: Migrations: changing a live database safely
summary: How schema changes travel from your laptop to production as files in git, and how to change a table without breaking the app that is using it.
youWillLearn: Why "works locally, breaks in production" happens with databases
What a migration file is, and how the database remembers which ones ran
Why you never edit an applied migration or click changes into production
The expand and contract pattern for renames and removals without downtime

glossary.app server: A computer, somewhere else, that runs the app's own code. Notely's runs on Vercel.
glossary.production: The live version of the app that real users like Maya use, as opposed to the copy on your laptop.
glossary.migration: A small file, usually SQL, that changes the database schema one step, kept in git and run in order on every database.
glossary.Supabase CLI: Supabase's command-line tool. It runs a local copy of your project and manages migration files.
glossary.migration history: A table inside the database that lists which migration files have already been applied.
glossary.schema drift: When a database's real shape no longer matches what the migration files describe, usually after a manual change.
glossary.expand and contract: A way to change a schema in safe stages: add the new thing, move code and data over, then remove the old thing later.
glossary.backfill: Filling a new column for rows that already existed before it was added.
glossary.lock: A database making other queries wait while it changes a table, so they do not see a half-finished change.

steps.title: How Notely gets from your laptop to Maya
body: You build Notely on your laptop with Claude Code. Your laptop runs its own copy of the database, to try things safely. You push code to GitHub, where it is stored; Vercel then puts it on the app server.
The app server talks to the live database that holds Maya's notes. Live, for real users, is production.

scene.caption: Code goes from your laptop to GitHub to the app server, which uses the live database.

steps.title: Works on my laptop, breaks in production
body: Maya asks for pinned notes. Claude Code adds a pinned column to your laptop's database and builds the feature. It works. You push, the new code goes live, and requests start failing: column notes.pinned does not exist.
The code traveled. The column did not. Two copies of the database, two different shapes.
changes: ~ Your Laptop: its database has the pinned column
~ Database: the live one never got it
~ Failed requests 0 → 120 / min

scene.caption: The code reached production. The column did not.

steps.title: Schema changes as files, in git
body: The fix: never change a database's shape by hand. Write each change as a small SQL file, a migration, and commit it to GitHub next to the code.
The Supabase CLI, a command-line tool, creates the file with a timestamp in its name, so files sort in order. Every database runs the same files, in the same order.

code.caption: Existing rows get false, so notes made before the change keep working.

callout.text: A logbook of recipe changes. Instead of cooking from memory, you write each change on a dated card. Any kitchen that follows the cards in order makes the same dish.

changes: ~ GitHub: now holds the migration file next to the code
+ GitHub → Database line: files run in order
~ Unapplied files 0 → 1

scene.caption: Migration files live in git, waiting to run on the live database.

steps.title: The database remembers what ran
body: Each database keeps a migration history: a small table listing every migration already applied. Supabase keeps it in supabase_migrations.schema_migrations.
supabase db push compares your folder with that list and runs only the new files, in order. Run it twice and the second run does nothing.

code.code:
# rebuild your laptop's database from every migration
supabase db reset

# apply new migrations to the live project
supabase db push

changes: ~ Unapplied files 1 → 0
~ Database: now has the pinned column
~ Failed requests 120 → 0 / min

scene.caption: The live database runs only the file it has not seen. The feature works.

steps.title: Never edit history, never click-ops
body: Two habits break migrations. Editing a file that already ran: the database will not run it again, so your change never arrives. Write a new migration instead.
Clicking a change into Supabase's dashboard (its web page for the database): now the live database has a shape no file describes. That is schema drift.

callout.text: Already clicked a change into the dashboard? Bring it back into git: supabase db pull writes the live schema into a new migration file. Then commit it.

changes: + Dashboard: Supabase's web page for changing the database
~ Database: now has a change no file describes

scene.caption: A dashboard edit changes the live database but no file. The copies drift apart.

steps.title: Old code and new schema overlap
body: A migration and a deploy never land at the same instant. For a while, old and new versions of Notely's code run side by side, on one database.
Say one migration renames title to heading. The new code is happy. The old code still asks for title, and fails. Adding is safe; renaming or removing breaks someone.
changes: − Your Laptop, GitHub and Dashboard: we zoom into one deploy
~ App Server → Old Code: still running for a while
+ New Code: the next version, rolling out
~ Failed requests 0 → 60 / min

scene.caption: Renaming title to heading in one go: the old code still running breaks.

steps.title: Expand: add the new, keep the old
body: The safe pattern is expand and contract. Expand first: add heading as a new column, and leave title alone.
Old code keeps reading title, so nothing breaks. New code writes both columns, so every new note fills both. Each step is safe to deploy on its own.

code.code: alter table notes add column heading text;

changes: ~ Database: title and heading, side by side
~ Old Code works again
~ Failed requests 60 → 0 / min

scene.caption: Both columns exist. Old and new code both work.

steps.title: Backfill, switch, then contract
body: Old notes have an empty heading, so a backfill copies each title into it. Then new code reads only heading.
Contract last: once no running code uses title, a later migration, shipped with a later deploy, drops it. More steps, no downtime.

callout.text: When Claude Code changes the schema, check: is there a new file in supabase/migrations, not a dashboard click or an edited old file? Does it rename or drop anything running code still uses? Ask: "Is this safe while the old code is still live?"

changes: − Old Code: fully replaced by New Code
~ Database: backfilled, then title dropped

scene.caption: Only the new code is left, so the old column can finally go.

steps.title: Big tables, long locks
body: Some changes make Postgres take a lock: while it rewrites a table, other queries wait. On a small table nobody notices. With millions of rows, Notely freezes.
Usual suspects: building an index (use create index concurrently), adding not null to an existing column, changing a column's type. And drop is forever, so have a backup first.

callout.text: Supabase migrations only move forward: there is no automatic undo. To reverse a change you write a new migration, and dropped data does not come back that way. Try destructive changes on a copy first.

changes: ~ Database: locked while a big change runs
~ New Code waits on every query
~ Query wait 5 → 30,000 ms

scene.caption: A big table is locked. Every query waits.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: Every schema change is a migration file in git, run in order on every database. The migration history makes sure each file runs once. Never edit an applied file, never click changes into production.
Old and new code overlap during a deploy, so expand first, contract later, and watch for locks on big tables.
changes: ~ Database: unlocked, one shape everywhere
~ Query wait 30,000 → 5 ms

scene.caption: Small, ordered steps that each keep the app working.

quiz.question: Right after a deploy, Notely's logs show column notes.pinned does not exist. It works locally. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Vercel cached an old build of the code.
options.why: The error comes from the database, not the code: the new code is running, and the column is missing.

options.text: The migration that adds pinned was never applied to production.
options.why: Local and production have different shapes. Apply the migration (supabase db push) and make that part of every deploy.

options.text: Postgres does not allow yes/no columns named pinned.
options.why: It does. The same query works locally, which points at a difference between the two databases.

quiz.question: You spot a mistake in a migration file that already ran on production last week. What do you do?

options.text: Fix the old file and push again.
options.why: Production's migration history says that file already ran, so it will not run it again. The fix never arrives.

options.text: Fix it in the production dashboard.
options.why: That creates schema drift: production now differs from what your files describe.

options.text: Write a new migration that corrects it.
options.why: History only moves forward. A new file reaches every database, in order, the same way.

quiz.question: Claude Code proposes one migration, alter table notes rename column title to heading;, shipped in the same deploy as code that reads heading. What is the risk?

options.text: During the rollout, the old code still asks for title and fails.
options.why: Old and new code overlap. Add heading, write both, backfill, switch reads, then drop title later.

options.text: Postgres cannot rename columns that contain data.
options.why: It can, and quickly. The danger is the running code that still expects the old name.

options.text: There is no risk, because migrations run before the deploy.
options.why: Even then, the old version keeps serving requests until the new one is fully live.

takeaways: Every schema change is a migration file in git, applied in order to every database.
The database keeps a migration history, so each file runs exactly once.
Never edit an applied migration and never click changes into production. Write a new migration.
Old and new code overlap during deploys: expand first, contract in a later deploy.
On big tables, ask about locks, and take a backup before any drop.
